lessons.title: Branding Basics at MAD
lessons.grammar: Adjectives before nouns (adjetivo antes do substantivo)
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to talk about a brand, a logo, and a color palette in simple English.
lessons.intro: MAD is a creative agency. We build brands for our clients. A brand is the face of a company. We design logos, colors, and fonts. We also make mood boards for new ideas. Clients like Verizon, Toyota, and LolaVie trust our work. Our team works in Miami, Tampa, and São Paulo. At MAD, we always raise the bar.

vocab.example: MAD builds a strong brand.
The new logo is red and white.
A brand identity shows who the company is.
Our color palette has three colors.
We make a mood board before we design.
We choose a clean font for the logo.
The client loves the new design.
We launch a big campaign in São Paulo.

lessons.situation: Leia esta cena real do estúdio da MAD. Imagine que você está lá.
lessons.context: It is Monday morning at the MAD studio in São Paulo. The team opens a new mood board for a client. They look at colors, fonts, and old logos. The creative director says, "Let's raise the bar on this brand."
lessons.grammarDetail:
Em inglês, o adjetivo vem ANTES do substantivo. Em português, o adjetivo geralmente vem DEPOIS. Por exemplo, dizemos "uma marca forte" em português, mas em inglês é "a strong brand" (forte + marca). O adjetivo nunca muda no plural: "strong brands" e não "strongs brands". Então a ordem é sempre: adjetivo + substantivo.

  • a strong brand (uma marca forte)
  • a clean logo (um logo limpo)
  • a big campaign (uma campanha grande)
lessons.grammarCriticalQuestion: What makes a brand strong? Think about a brand you like.

lessons.title: SEO Basics at the MAD Tampa Team
lessons.grammar: Present Simple para rotinas e fatos (Presente Simples)
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to use basic SEO words in English and talk about keywords, Google ranking, and website traffic.
lessons.intro: At MAD, the Tampa team works on digital marketing. SEO means Search Engine Optimization. SEO helps a website rank higher on Google. The team chooses good keywords for each page. Good keywords bring more organic traffic. More traffic means more visitors for our clients. The team writes simple and clear content. This content helps people find the client on Google.

vocab.example: We choose the best keyword for the page.
Our ranking on Google is better this month.
People use search to find new products.
The website traffic is growing every week.
Good content helps the website rank higher.
Organic traffic comes from free search results.
This page has the right keywords.
Google shows our client in the first result.

lessons.situation: Leia esta cena real do dia a dia do time de marketing da MAD em Tampa.
lessons.context: It is Monday morning at the MAD Tampa office. The marketing team opens the report for a client. The organic traffic is up, and the keywords rank higher on Google. Maria says, "Great work! Now we need more content for the blog page." The team starts a new SEO plan for the week.
lessons.grammarDetail:
Usamos o Present Simple para falar de rotinas e fatos, como as tarefas diárias do time de marketing. Em inglês, com he/she/it (ele/ela/isso) acrescentamos -s no verbo: 'The team writes content' (O time escreve conteúdo). Com I/you/we/they não muda: 'We write content' (Nós escrevemos conteúdo). Atenção: em português dizemos 'nós escrevemos / ela escreve', mas em inglês só a 3ª pessoa do singular (he/she/it) ganha o -s.

  • The team chooses good keywords every week. (O time escolhe boas palavras-chave toda semana.)
  • Google ranks the best pages first. (O Google posiciona as melhores páginas primeiro.)
  • We track the website traffic every day. (Nós acompanhamos o tráfego do site todos os dias.)
lessons.grammarCriticalQuestion: Why are good keywords important for a client's website on Google?

lessons.title: Shipping the Web: Dev Workflow at MAD
lessons.grammar: Present Perfect for completed work (have/has + past participle)
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to describe your web development workflow in English — talking about features, deploys, pull requests, code reviews, and bugs during daily meetings and sprints.
lessons.intro: At MAD, we build web platforms, apps, and interactive experiences — sometimes with a bit of AR/VR or AI on top. A typical project runs in sprints, usually two weeks long. Front-end developers work mostly with React, while the back-end team builds APIs in Node. Every morning we have a quick daily meeting to share what we did, what we're doing, and what's blocking us. When a feature is ready, we open a pull request so a teammate can run a code review before it goes live. Once the review is approved, we merge the code and deploy it to production. If a bug shows up, we open a ticket, reproduce it, and fix it fast. Speaking clear English about this process keeps the whole team aligned, especially when clients are international.

vocab.example: We deploy the new feature on Friday afternoon.
All our code lives in the same repository on GitHub.
I opened a pull request and asked Bruno to review it.
She left a few comments during the code review.
There's a bug in the login form on mobile.
We planned six tasks for this sprint.
The client requested a new search feature.
The front-end calls the /users endpoint to load the list.

lessons.situation: Uma cena real de daily na MAD.
lessons.context: It's 9:30 and the team starts the daily standup. Marina says: "Yesterday I finished the checkout feature and opened a pull request. Today I'll start the code review for João's branch. I'm a bit blocked because the staging server is down." João adds that he fixed the cache bug and will deploy the fix after lunch. The tech lead nods and asks everyone to keep their tickets updated on the board. In five minutes, the standup is done and everyone is back to coding.
lessons.grammarDetail:
Use the present perfect to talk about work that is done but still relevant now — typical in daily standups. Form: have/has + past participle. We say "I have finished the feature" / "She has deployed the fix". Em português, costuma traduzir como "já terminei" / "acabei de publicar". Use "already", "just" and "yet" with it: "I've already merged the PR", "She's just pushed the code", "We haven't deployed yet". Compare with simple past, which needs a finished time: "I finished it yesterday" (specific time) vs "I've finished it" (focus on the result now).

  • I have opened the pull request, so you can review it now.
  • She has already fixed the bug on the login screen.
  • We haven't deployed the new feature to production yet.
lessons.grammarCriticalQuestion: When you give your update in a daily standup, how do you keep it short but clear so the rest of the team understands what you've done and what is blocking you?

lessons.title: Running the Account: Meetings, Timelines & Keeping Clients Happy
lessons.grammar: Polite requests with would / could / I was wondering
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to lead a client meeting in English, give a clear status update, talk about timelines and deliverables, and make polite requests when you need to push back on scope or deadlines.
lessons.intro: At MAD, account managers are the bridge between the client and the creative and tech teams. Every project starts with a briefing and a kickoff meeting, where we align on scope, budget, and timeline. After that, your job is to keep things moving: chasing approvals, sending status updates, and managing expectations on both sides. International clients like Verizon and Toyota expect clear, confident communication in English. They want to know what is on track, what is at risk, and when the next deliverable lands. A good account manager protects the relationship and the deadline at the same time. When something slips, you flag it early and propose a solution instead of an excuse. This lesson gives you the language to handle those conversations like a pro.

vocab.example: The client sent the briefing, so we can start scoping the work.
Let's set up a kickoff meeting with the whole team next Tuesday.
The first deliverable is the campaign concept, due Friday.
That request is outside the scope we agreed on.
We agreed on a deadline with the client for the end of the month.
I'll send a status update before the weekly call.
We need sign-off from every stakeholder before we launch.
I'll send a quick follow-up email to confirm the next steps.

lessons.situation: Leia esta cena de uma call com cliente.
lessons.context: It's the weekly status call with the Verizon team. The account manager opens by running through the timeline: the creative concept is approved, but production is two days behind because of a late feedback round. The client asks whether the launch date is still safe. The account manager confirms the deadline holds and explains the plan to recover the time. She then asks the client to confirm the final stakeholder list so nothing gets stuck in approvals. Before closing, she promises a follow-up email with the updated schedule and the next deliverables.
lessons.grammarDetail:
Em reuniões com clientes, pedidos diretos como 'Send me the brief' soam abruptos. Use forms more polite to sound professional. 'Could you...?' and 'Would you mind...?' are softer than the imperative. 'I was wondering if you could...' is even more polite and great for sensitive requests, like asking for an extension or extra budget. Note: after 'Would you mind' we use the -ing form ('Would you mind sending...?').

  • Could you send over the updated briefing by Thursday?
  • Would you mind confirming the final stakeholder list today?
  • I was wondering if we could push the deadline by two days.
lessons.grammarCriticalQuestion: A client keeps adding new requests that go beyond the agreed scope, but you don't want to damage the relationship. How would you raise this in a meeting? What polite phrases would you use to protect the timeline and the budget while keeping the client on your side?

lessons.title: From Brief to Final Render: Speaking the Language of High-End Production
lessons.grammar: Hedging and diplomatic distancing in production notes
lessons.objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to talk through the entire MAD production pipeline in confident, idiomatic English — pitching a concept, walking a client through a cut, giving precise notes on color, sound and motion, and framing the trade-offs behind an immersive MAD Arts experience.
lessons.intro: At MAD, nothing reaches the screen by accident — every frame is the result of a deliberate chain of decisions that begins long before the camera rolls. Pre-production is where the work is really won or lost: we lock the concept, break down the script, build the storyboard and circulate a call sheet so that the shoot itself becomes the easy part. On set, the priority is to capture footage with enough latitude that post never feels boxed in. Once the material is in the edit, we move from a rough cut that interrogates structure toward a fine cut that defends every beat. Color grading and sound design are not finishing touches; they are where tone, mood and intention are finally negotiated. Motion graphics and compositing thread the brand through the piece without ever upstaging the story. When we render and package deliverables, we are translating one master into a dozen formats, each with its own constraints. And on the MAD Arts side, the same discipline scales up into projection mapping and immersive installations, where the medium is no longer a rectangle but an entire room. The craft is the same; only the canvas changes.

vocab.example: We reviewed hours of footage before committing to a rough cut.
The rough cut is ugly on purpose — it's there to test whether the story holds.
She pushed the color grading toward a colder palette to make the interior feel clinical.
The sound design carries half the emotion in that sequence; the picture is almost incidental.
We kept the motion graphics restrained so they wouldn't fight the live action.
The client signed off, so we're now mastering the full set of deliverables.
The projection mapping had to be calibrated on-site to the exact contours of the façade.
MAD Arts built an immersive experience where the visuals respond to where the visitor stands.

lessons.situation: Read this post-production review scene and notice the diplomatic, precise register the team uses.
lessons.context: It's the second post review for a MAD Arts installation, and the room is split-screening the fine cut against the projection test. The director leans in: 'The grade is beautiful, but the highlights are clipping the moment the dancer crosses the light — can we pull those back a touch?' The colorist nods, already isolating the window. On the audio side, the sound designer flags that the low-end rumble is masking the dialogue stems, so they agree to duck the bed by a few dB rather than re-record. The producer, watching the clock, asks the only question that matters: 'If we lock picture by Thursday, are the deliverables still realistic for the opening?' Everyone knows the honest answer is 'tight, but yes — if no new notes land.'
lessons.grammarDetail:
Senior producers rarely give notes as blunt commands — that reads as aggressive and shuts down collaboration. Instead, English softens directives through hedging: modal verbs (could, might, would), tentative verbs (I'd suggest, I wonder if, I'm not sure we need), and grammatical distancing such as 'we might want to consider pulling that back' rather than 'pull that back.' The past-tense modal 'would' and the conditional frame ('if we did X, we'd gain Y') create psychological distance that makes a strong opinion feel like a shared option rather than an order. Notice too the use of 'a touch,' 'slightly,' 'a hair' as minimizers that signal you respect the work already done. The skill is calibration: be unmistakably clear about what you want changed, but phrase it so the room stays open. 'The pacing dies in the middle — fix it' lands very differently from 'I feel like we lose a little momentum in the middle third; could we tighten it?'

  • I wonder if we might pull the saturation back just a touch in the wides.
  • We could consider re-cutting that transition, though I'm not sure it's worth the time at this stage.
  • If we leaned into the sound design there, I think we'd carry the emotion without needing the extra shot.
lessons.grammarCriticalQuestion: In an immersive MAD Arts piece, the 'edit' is no longer something the audience watches in a fixed order — they move through it. How does that change the way you think about pacing, story and the notes you'd give in a review? Is a producer still shaping a narrative, or designing a possibility space?
